client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away a few weeks ago. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of something and then just completely lose my train of thought, and it's starting to affect my performance. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing's going to bring her back.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — grief like this can make even the simplest tasks feel impossible, and what you're experiencing at work makes complete sense given what you're carrying right now. You're right that nothing will bring her back, and I don't want to promise that talking will "fix" that, but sometimes it can help us find a way to hold the pain so it doesn't feel quite so overwhelming on its own. What was she like to you — what do you find yourself missing most?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: She was just... the one person who never made me feel like I had to explain myself, you know? I could show up at her house upset or confused and she'd just make tea and sit with me, and somehow that was enough. Now when things get hard at work or I feel overwhelmed, I keep reaching for my phone to call her, and then I remember, and it's like losing her all over again.
therapist: What you're describing — that moment of reaching for the phone and then remembering — sounds like one of the most painful parts of grief, almost like a small loss happening over and over again. She clearly offered you something really rare: a place where you could just *be*, without having to perform or explain yourself. I'm wondering, as you talk about her now, what does it feel like to put that into words?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, it feels strange — like I'm not used to actually describing her out loud to someone, and part of me feels guilty for even trying, like I'm reducing her to a few sentences. But there's also something that feels almost like relief, which then makes me feel guilty too, like I shouldn't be getting any relief from this. I don't really know what to do with that.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — feeling like relief is somehow a betrayal — is actually one of the most common and painful paradoxes of grief, and it doesn't mean you loved her any less. Relief can simply mean that being seen and understood, even in memory, still carries some of her warmth. I'm curious, do you think she would have judged you for finding even a small moment of ease in remembering her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: No, she definitely wouldn't have judged me — that's actually kind of the whole point of who she was. But knowing that in my head and actually feeling it are two really different things, and I'm not sure just reminding myself of that is going to make the guilt go away. It's like I understand the logic but it doesn't reach wherever the guilt is actually living.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that gap between knowing something intellectually and actually *feeling* it in your body is real, and it's one of the reasons grief can be so exhausting. The guilt isn't living in the part of you that understands logic; it's living somewhere deeper, maybe in the part that's still just really missing her. I'm wondering, when you notice that guilt showing up, whereabouts do you actually feel it — is it more of a thought, or does it land somewhere in your body too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It's mostly in my chest, like a kind of heaviness that just sits there, especially when I'm at work and I lose focus and then remember why I can't concentrate. I've never really thought about it that way before, as something physical, and I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with that information — like, does noticing it actually change anything? It still feels pretty stuck.
therapist: Noticing it doesn't make it disappear, but it does mean you're no longer just being swept along by it without knowing what's happening — and that's actually the first step toward having some relationship with it, rather than it just having you. There's something tender in the way you're describing this, like you're being very careful and quiet with yourself right now, which makes sense given how much you're carrying. What do you think that heaviness in your chest most needs from you in those moments at work — even if there's no perfect answer?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it probably just needs me to acknowledge it instead of panicking and trying to push through like nothing's happening, but that feels really hard to do at work where there are people around and deadlines and I'm already worried about what my manager thinks of my performance lately. It's like I can't afford to stop and feel it there, even for a second. I guess I'm scared that if I actually let myself acknowledge it in the middle of the workday, I'll just fall apart completely.
therapist: That fear of falling apart makes so much sense, and it's actually very common — but it's worth gently questioning whether acknowledging something for a moment truly leads to collapse, or whether that's a story the anxiety is telling you to keep you "safe." What you just described — that quiet, almost careful way you're holding all of this even as you talk about it — suggests you might have more steadiness in you than you're giving yourself credit for right now. What do you think a very small acknowledgment might actually look like in practice, something that wouldn't require you to fall apart — maybe just a breath, or a private word to yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Maybe something like just saying to myself "I miss her" and letting that be true for a second instead of immediately trying to get back on task — but even as I say that, I'm not convinced it won't just open a door I can't close again in the middle of a Tuesday afternoon. I think part of me has been treating the grief like it's this dangerous thing that needs to be contained, and I'm not sure I trust yet that a small acknowledgment stays small. It makes sense as an idea, but I've never actually tested it.
therapist: The way you just described that — treating grief like something dangerous that needs to be contained — feels like a really significant insight, and I notice there's something almost fragile in how you're holding it, like you're speaking carefully around something that feels bigger than the words. You've never tested it, which means the fear of the door not closing is still just a prediction, not a fact — and predictions made in grief are often our mind's way of trying to protect us from more pain. What do you think it would mean about you, or about your grief, if it turned out that a small acknowledgment *did* stay small?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think it would mean that maybe I've been giving the grief more power over me than it actually has, which is both a relief to consider and also kind of unsettling — like, if I don't need to be so afraid of it, then what have I been doing these past few weeks? It might also mean that I've been so focused on containing it that I haven't actually been letting myself grieve her properly, and I'm not sure how I feel about that realization. It's a lot to sit with.
therapist: That realization — that containment might have come at the cost of actually grieving her — is a really courageous thing to sit with, and it makes sense that it feels unsettling alongside the relief. The weeks you've spent trying to hold it together weren't wasted; they were you doing the best you could with something enormous, and that deserves some gentleness rather than judgment. I'm curious — when you imagine actually grieving her "properly," whatever that means to you, what does that picture look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I'm not sure I even know what grieving properly looks like — I think I've always associated it with crying a lot, and I haven't really cried much, which is another thing I've been feeling guilty about. Maybe it looks like letting myself talk about her more, not just to you but to people who knew her, though that feels scary because I don't want to burden anyone or make things awkward. I guess I've been so alone with this that I'm not even sure I remember how to let someone else in.
therapist: The guilt about not crying is so common, and yet grief has never had just one face — talking about her, remembering her, even that heaviness in your chest, those are all grief too. What strikes me is that you just named something really important: that you've been so alone with this, and yet here you are, carefully and quietly letting someone in right now. I'm wondering, what made it feel possible to do that today, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think part of it was just that I was desperate enough to try, because the not-focusing-at-work thing is getting bad enough that I couldn't keep pretending everything was fine. And you didn't immediately try to fix it or tell me what I should be feeling, which I wasn't expecting — I think I came in ready to be told to do breathing exercises or something and then feel like it hadn't worked. I'm still not sure how much I trust this process, but I guess today felt a little less like talking into a void than I thought it would.
therapist: What you just said — that this felt a little less like talking into a void — is actually a really meaningful thing to acknowledge, and I don't want to gloss over it, because it sounds like being truly heard has felt pretty rare for you lately. It makes sense that trust in this process would come slowly, especially when you arrived braced for something that felt more like a checklist than a conversation. I'm glad desperation brought you here today, and I'm curious what you might want to bring into the space next time, now that you know a little more about what this can feel like.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
